OPENING_CONTEXT

1. Counting begins with one, the smallest thing you can point at.
2. Two is what you get when you notice a second thing beside the first.
3. Three makes a pattern, and patterns make counting feel natural.
4. Four fingers and a thumb make a hand, and a hand makes five.
5. Children often count on their fingers before they count in their heads.
6. Six is the first number that is the sum of its proper divisors.
7. Seven days make a week, a count most of us never question.
8. Eight bits make a byte, so computers count in small bundles.
9. Nine is the last single digit in our everyday system.
10. Ten fingers are a likely reason base ten became common.
11. Eleven breaks the pattern of tidy names in English.
12. Twelve eggs make a dozen, a count that survives in every kitchen.
13. Thirteen has a reputation it did nothing to earn.
14. Fourteen days make a fortnight, a word that is nearly gone.
15. Fifteen minutes is a quarter of an hour, and a common meeting slot.
16. Sixteen is two to the fourth power, a favorite of programmers.
17. Seventeen is prime, and it sits awkwardly between friendlier numbers.
18. Eighteen is a number many places treat as the age of adulthood.
19. Nineteen years make a Metonic cycle in the lunar calendar.
20. Twenty is a score, as in "four score and seven years ago."
21. Counting sheep is a way to fall asleep, though the evidence is thin.
22. Tally marks group in fives, with a slash across four lines.
23. Roman numerals count with I, V, X, L, C, D and M.
24. Roman numerals have no zero, so they cannot show an empty place.
25. Zero was a late and radical addition to the counting story.
26. Counting from zero is why programmers number array positions from 0.
27. Counting from one is what everyone else does, and neither habit is wrong.
28. A fencepost error happens when you count posts and gaps as the same thing.
29. Ten fence posts hold up only nine sections of fence.
30. Counting the days between two dates raises the question of whether to include both ends.
31. Counting by twos gives the even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, and onward.
32. Counting by fives is how we read the minute marks on a clock.
33. Counting by tens is the quickest way to cover a large distance.
34. Counting by hundreds turns a long road into a short one.
35. Counting backwards is a countdown, and countdowns build tension.
36. A rocket launch counts down so that everyone shares the same zero.
37. Hide and seek relies on counting to a number the seeker agrees to.
38. Counting aloud keeps a group in step, as in marching and rowing.
39. A conductor counts a bar of music before the orchestra plays.
40. A waltz counts in threes, and a march counts in twos or fours.
41. Counting syllables is how a haiku gets its shape.
42. Counting words is how an essay stays within its limit.
43. Counting calories is a habit some people keep and others avoid.
44. Counting steps turned walking into a game for millions of people.
45. Counting breaths is a gentle way to settle a restless mind.
46. Counting to ten is old advice for anyone about to lose their temper.
47. A census is counting at the scale of a whole country.
48. A ballot count decides who wins and how much people trust the result.
49. Counting votes twice is a sensible safeguard, not an insult.
50. Counting inventory is how a shop learns what it truly has.
51. A cycle count checks a few items each day instead of everything at once.
52. A tally of money at the end of a shift is called "counting the till."
53. Counting change back to a customer used to be a daily skill.
54. Counting cards is legal but unwelcome in most casinos.
55. Counting stars is a hopeless task that people still enjoy trying.
56. About 2,500 stars are visible to the naked eye on a clear, dark night.
57. Counting grains of sand is a classic example of a huge but finite number.
58. Archimedes wrote a treatise on counting the grains of sand that would fill the universe.
59. A googol is a one followed by a hundred zeros.
60. A googolplex is a one followed by a googol of zeros, which cannot be written out.
61. Infinity is not a number you reach by counting, however long you go.
62. Counting never ends, because every number has a successor.
63. Some infinities are larger than others, as Cantor showed.
64. The whole numbers and the even numbers can be paired off one for one.
65. That pairing means they have the same size, which feels strange at first.
66. The real numbers cannot be paired with the whole numbers, so they are uncountable.
67. Counting in binary uses only 0 and 1.
68. In binary, the number two is written 10.
69. In binary, the number five is written 101.
70. In binary, the number ten is written 1010.
71. Counting in hexadecimal runs 0 to 9, then A to F.
72. In hexadecimal, the letter F stands for fifteen.
73. Counting in octal uses only the digits 0 through 7.
74. Counting in base sixty gave us sixty minutes and sixty seconds.
75. The Babylonians counted in base sixty over four thousand years ago.
76. The Maya counted in base twenty, probably from fingers and toes.
77. French still carries traces of base twenty in "quatre-vingts," or four twenties.
78. Some languages have words for only one, two, and many.
79. Researchers have studied cultures with very few number words and found real limits on exact counting.
80. Counting small groups at a glance is called subitizing.
81. Most people can subitize up to about four items.
82. Beyond four, we switch to counting one by one or in groups.
83. Dice and dominoes use patterns so that we can read a count at a glance.
84. Counting objects in groups, called chunking, speeds up long counts.
85. Counting by chunks of five or ten makes a long row of items manageable.
86. A common trick for counting a crowd is to count one block and multiply.
87. Estimating a count is a skill separate from counting exactly.
88. Estimating well means being roughly right instead of precisely wrong.
89. A jar of jellybeans is the classic estimation puzzle.
90. The average of many guesses at a jar's contents is often surprisingly close.
91. Counting the same set twice and getting two answers means one count is wrong.
92. A good habit is to count again in a different order and compare.
93. Counting in a different order should never change the total.
94. That fact, called the invariance of count, is something children learn early.
95. Another early lesson is that the last number said tells you how many there are.
96. This idea has a name, the cardinality principle.
97. A child who can recite numbers has not necessarily grasped what they mean.
98. Matching one number word to each object is called one-to-one correspondence.
99. Skipping an object or counting it twice breaks that correspondence.
100. Pointing at each object while counting helps prevent both mistakes.
101. Moving counted objects to a separate pile helps too.
102. Counting books on a shelf is easy because the books stay put.
103. Counting people in motion is harder, since they move and swap places.
104. A turnstile counts people mechanically and never loses its place.
105. A clicker counter does the same job for a bouncer at a door.
106. A pedometer counts steps by sensing motion.
107. An odometer counts the distance a car has traveled.
108. A rotary counter on old machinery used wheels of digits that roll over.
109. A rollover happens when a counter passes its largest value and wraps to zero.
110. The Y2K scare was partly a counting problem with two-digit years.
111. Unix time counts the seconds since the first of January, 1970.
112. A 32-bit signed counter of those seconds runs out in January 2038.
113. A counter that overflows can produce bugs that look like magic.
114. A loop in a program often uses a counter to keep track of its place.
115. A counter that never reaches its limit makes an infinite loop.
116. Off-by-one errors are among the most common mistakes in code.
117. A counter that starts at the wrong number produces an answer one too high or low.
118. A good test checks the boundaries: zero, one, and the largest allowed value.
119. A database can count rows with a single query.
120. Counting rows in a huge table can be slow if the database must scan it all.
121. Some systems keep an approximate count to answer faster.
122. A distributed counter must agree on a total even when machines disagree on timing.
123. Counting unique visitors is harder than counting visits, since you must recognize repeats.
124. Probabilistic counters can estimate unique counts using very little memory.
125. Counting is the base of probability, which starts with counting possible outcomes.
126. Two coin flips have four equally likely outcomes.
127. Three coin flips have eight outcomes, since each flip doubles the count.
128. A deck of fifty-two cards can be arranged in more ways than there are atoms on Earth.
129. Counting arrangements is called permutations, and counting selections is called combinations.
130. Choosing two people from five can be done in ten ways.
131. Factorials count the ways to line up a set of objects.
132. Five objects can be lined up in a hundred and twenty ways.
133. Ten objects can be lined up in over three million ways.
134. Pascal's triangle is a table of counts for choosing items from a set.
135. Each number in Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two numbers above it.
136. The Fibonacci sequence counts rabbits in a puzzle from the year 1202.
137. It runs 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, and so on.
138. Counting the petals of many flowers often turns up a Fibonacci number.
139. Prime numbers are those with exactly two divisors, and they never run out.
140. Counting primes below a given number is a long-standing research question.
141. Counting the divisors of a number reveals whether it is prime or composite.
142. Counting in modular arithmetic wraps around, like the hours on a clock.
143. Thirteen o'clock on a twelve-hour clock lands on one.
144. Leap years add a day every four years, with exceptions for centuries.
145. Counting the days in a month is a rhyme many people learned as children.
146. Knuckles can be used to remember which months have thirty-one days.
147. Counting weeks in a year gives fifty-two, plus a day or two left over.
148. Counting down to a holiday makes the waiting feel shorter or longer, depending on the person.
149. Advent calendars count down the days to a holiday with a little treat each time.
150. Counting your blessings is advice about attention more than arithmetic.
151. Counting on someone means trusting them, a meaning that has nothing to do with numbers.
152. Counting out loud with a child is one of the first shared lessons in math.
153. Songs and rhymes like "One, two, buckle my shoe" make counting stick.
154. Counting games like hopscotch turn practice into play.
155. A good teacher lets learners count real objects before moving to symbols.
156. From objects, learners move to pictures, then to numerals, then to ideas.
157. Counting is the first math most people learn and the last they ever stop using.
158. Every large number was built, in principle, by adding one again and again.
159. Every measurement, in the end, is a count of some chosen unit.
160. And so the list ends where it began, with the simple act of counting one more.
